claims.text: Controlled isothermal annealing at 300–500°C promotes diffusion-driven Mg segregation in MgTiZn-based lightweight high-entropy alloys.
Mg segregation induces nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates form both at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates disrupt the continuity of native passivating oxide films.
The relevant native passivating films include TiO2-rich layers.
Disruption of passivating films by intermetallic precipitates causes loss of corrosion resistance.
Disruption of passivating films by intermetallic precipitates causes loss of high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The kinetics of intermetallic formation depend on annealing time and temperature.
Slow cooling followed by extended annealing accelerates the transition from a metastable solid solution to a phase-separated microstructure containing connected intermetallic networks.
The initial as-quenched alloy is a metastable solid solution.
The initial as-quenched alloy contains minimal intermetallic phases.
The initial as-quenched state has optimal corrosion and oxidation characteristics.
Temperatures from 300°C to 500°C represent service-relevant regimes for the proposed alloy.
Mg-rich intermetallic formation becomes pronounced near a threshold temperature of approximately 450°C.
Above approximately 450°C, intermetallic volume fraction increases with annealing time.
Annealing-induced intermetallic evolution will produce higher corrosion current density than in the rapid-quenched metastable state.
Annealing-induced intermetallic evolution will diminish oxide-scale integrity relative to the rapid-quenched metastable state.
Compositional inhomogeneities could alter the kinetics of the proposed transformation.
